speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. You mentioned a pruritic rash, fever, rhinorrhea, and headache; were these symptoms starting together or did the rash appear after the other symptoms began? REQUEST TEST: CBC, CMP, CRP. REQUEST IMAGES: Rash_close_up.

speaker: Doctor
text: The lab results and images show normal readings, so your symptoms may not be from a bacterial infection or a specific skin pathology yet. Since you mentioned rhinorrhea and headache along with the rash, could you tell me if you have been in close contact with anyone who recently developed a similar rash?

speaker: Patient
text: 11-year-old girl. The patient has been experiencing a mildly pruritic rash on her trunk and extremities for 2 days. One week ago, she developed symptoms of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and headache. A facial rash appeared 4 days later, sparing the perioral area.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Roseola Infantum (Exanthem Subitum). The clinical picture of a child with one week of prodromal fever (with upper respiratory symptoms) followed by the sudden appearance of a rash as the fever breaks is classic for this condition, caused by HHV-6 or HHV-7. The rash typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the extremities, often sparing the face initially or appearing later, and is usually mild and pruritic. No further tests are needed as the diagnosis is clinically evident and the prognosis is excellent.
